references.text: A woman came to Jesus with an alabaster jar of expensive ointment and anointed his head while he was reclining at the table – a parallel account of a woman anointing Jesus.
A woman brought an alabaster jar of genuine, costly nard ointment and anointed Jesus' head in Mark's parallel account of the anointing.
John identifies Mary as the one who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, a direct reference to the action described in Luke 7:38.

Mary took genuine, costly nard ointment, anointed Jesus' feet, and wiped them with her hair – very close to the parallel account of the action in Luke 7:38, including the detail of wiping the feet with hair.
The psalmist says that he wets his bed with tears – the motif of tears as an expression of deep sorrow and repentance, just as the woman wept at Jesus' feet.

Jesus himself comments on the woman's actions in this passage: she wet his feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, kissed his feet, and anointed them with ointment – a direct explanation and elaboration of verse 38.

The immediate context: Jesus is reclining at the table at the house of the Pharisee Simon, and a sinful woman from the city comes with an alabaster jar of ointment – the introduction to the action in verse 38.
Paul mentions washing the feet of the saints as a characteristic of a godly widow – an act of humility and service that recalls the woman's action at Jesus' feet.
Jesus washes his disciples' feet – an act of deep humility connected with the feet, mirroring the humble action performed by the woman at Jesus' feet.
Bathsheba bowed down and threw herself before the king – an act of reverence at a person's feet, reminiscent of the woman's position at Jesus' feet.
